hints: Think about which two subshells electrons can be removed from when a transition metal forms ions, and how much energy difference there is between them.
walkthrough:
Picture where the electrons live**
Think of a transition metal like iron or copper. Its outer electrons are in the $\text{4s}$ orbital and the $\text{3d}$ orbitals. Even though one is n=3 and one is n=4, they sit almost at the same energy level, like two shelves at almost the same height.

Link similar energy to variable loss**
Because the energy gap is so tiny, removing a $\text{4s}$ electron costs about the same as removing a $\text{3d}$ electron. So the metal can lose different total numbers of electrons to give $+2$, $+3$, $+6$ and so on, all with stable arrangements.
Final answer: The $\text{3d}$ and $\text{4s}$ subshells are very close/similar in energy, so variable numbers of electrons can be removed with similar amounts of energy.

hints: Recall how most d-orbitals look with four lobes, then think what makes the $d_{z^2}$ orbital special along the z-axis.
walkthrough:
Remember the odd one out**
Four of the five d-orbitals look like a four leaf clover. The $3d_{z^2}$ is different. Imagine two balloons stretched up and down along the z-axis, meeting at the nucleus, with a flat doughnut ring squeezed around the middle in the xy-plane.

Place it on the axes**
Draw the long dumbbell shape exactly on the z-axis line given in Fig. 4.1, and add the small torus around the centre. That combination is the examiner standard for $d_{z^2}$.
Final answer: Sketch shows two lobes along the z-axis plus a central torus (doughnut) ring in the xy-plane, centred on origin.

hints: Start from the pale blue $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ and recall what happens when $\text{OH}^-$ ions remove water ligands as acid-base reaction versus when a new ligand simply swaps in.
Think of one classic reagent that gives a pale blue solid with $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, and two classic reagents that keep copper in solution but change its colour to deep blue or yellow.
Remember to balance charge and coordination number 6 or 4 when writing the copper product formulae for hydroxide, ammine and chloro complexes.
walkthrough:
Sort precipitation from substitution**
Keep the two ideas separate. Precipitation means $\text{OH}^-$ pulls protons off the coordinated water and neutral $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$ falls out as a solid. Ligand substitution means the $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are directly replaced but everything stays dissolved, just changing colour.

Build solution A answer**
Adding excess $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ to pale blue $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}(aq)$ gives a pale blue precipitate. Write it as $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$, which can also be shown hydrated as $[\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]$.

Build solution B answer**
Pick one familiar substitution. With excess concentrated ammonia you get a deep dark blue solution containing $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$. Alternatively with excess concentrated $\text{HCl}$ you get a yellow solution containing tetrahedral $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$. Either pair earns full credit.

Final answer: Solution A: $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{OH}^-$; observation: (pale) blue ppt.; product: $\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2$ or $[\text{Cu}(\text{OH})_2(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4]$.
Solution B: conc. $\text{NH}_3$ / $\text{NH}_3$ giving dark/deep blue solution, product $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$ OR conc. $\text{HCl}$ / $\text{Cl}^-$ giving yellow solution, product $[\text{CuCl}_4]^{2-}$.

hints: Work out the electron configuration of $\text{Ag}^+$ from Ag $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^1$ and see what happens to the d-subshell after losing one electron.
Recall the three steps needed for colour in complexes: splitting of d-orbitals, promotion of a d-electron, and absorption of visible light, then check which step is blocked here.
walkthrough:
Find the d-count**
Silver atom is $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^1$. Remove the $5s$ electron to make $\text{Ag}^+$, leaving $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}$. Every d-orbital is completely full, there is no vacancy.

Why full means colourless**
Colour comes when a d-electron absorbs visible light and jumps to a higher split d-orbital. If all d-orbitals are already full, that jump cannot happen. No light is absorbed, no colour is seen, so $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$ looks colourless.

Final answer: $\text{Ag}^+$ is $d^{10}$ / has a full complete d-subshell.
No d-electron can be promoted / no d-d transition is possible, so no visible light is absorbed.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.2, count how many N atoms in $en$ or in $dpys$ each have a lone pair available to donate.
Recall the general definition of any ligand as an electron pair donor, then extend it to what the prefix bi means for number of bonds to the same metal.
walkthrough:
Spot the two donor atoms**
Look at $en$, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. It has two N atoms, each with a lone pair. Look at $dpys$. It has two pyridine N atoms, each with a lone pair. Both can grab the metal at two points like a claw.

State the full definition**
A ligand donates lone pairs to a metal by dative covalent bonds. Bidentate simply means two such bonds from one ligand molecule to the same central metal ion, using its two lone pairs.
Final answer: A species with two lone pairs of electrons that form two dative covalent / coordinate bonds to a central metal atom / ion.

hints: Compare with $[\text{Ru}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^+$ which shows cis and trans, then ask why replacing four $\text{NH}_3$ with two N-N chelates creates an extra isomer.
Think about placing the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands opposite each other versus next to each other, and whether the cis arrangement with two chelate rings can be mirrored.
Remember that a bidentate N-N must occupy two adjacent octahedral positions, it can never span trans, so sketch the chelates as arcs linking cis sites.
walkthrough:
Fix the trans isomer**
Put the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands at top and bottom, trans to each other. The two $dpys$ ligands, shown as N-N arcs, then occupy the four equatorial positions. This is the highly symmetrical trans form, one of the three.

Fix the cis pair**
Now put the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands next to each other, at 90 degrees, cis. There are still two ways to wrap the two N-N chelates around the remaining four sites. They are mirror images, like left and right hands.

Show all three clearly**
Draw isomer 1 as trans-$\text{Cl}$. Draw isomer 2 and isomer 3 both as cis-$\text{Cl}$ but with the N-N arcs mirrored. That gives one trans plus a pair of optical isomers, three stereoisomers in total.

Final answer: Isomer 1: trans-$\text{Cl}$ isomer, both $\text{Cl}$ opposite, two N-N chelates in plane perpendicular.
Isomer 2 and Isomer 3: pair of cis-$\text{Cl}$ isomers (non-superimposable mirror images), both $\text{Cl}$ adjacent, with the two N-N chelates arranged as optical isomers.

hints: Use your answer to (e)(i), one relationship is about Cl being opposite or adjacent, the other is about the two cis structures being mirror images.
walkthrough:
Name both types**
The trans versus cis $\text{Cl}$ positions is cis-trans or geometrical isomerism. The two different cis forms that are non-superimposable mirror images show optical isomerism. $[\text{Ru}(dpys)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ shows both.
Final answer: Optical isomerism AND cis-trans / geometrical isomerism.

hints: Think about symmetry and bond dipoles for Ru-Cl bonds, when do two equal dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel?
walkthrough:
See why trans cancels**
In the trans isomer the two $\text{Ru-Cl}$ bond dipoles point exactly opposite, 180 degrees apart. They are equal and opposite so they cancel out. The cis isomer has them at 90 degrees so they add to give a net dipole. Therefore only the trans form is non-polar.
Final answer: The trans isomer is non-polar because the dipoles / partial charges cancel.
